series: Chess programs rated in play against people, 1966 to 1997 (hand-curated)
unit: USCF rating or USCF performance rating, as each point's measure and pool say (Deep Blue's: scale not stated). Human pools, not the engine lists' scales.
description: Landmark programs' ratings in human play, from the first program given a chess rating (Mac Hack VI) to Deep Blue, for the chess chart (src/viz/chess.js), which draws them as hollow markers apart from the engine lists in chess_elo.json. Each point is one rating or one event's performance rating, dated, with its pool and measure, taken by hand from Wikipedia's articles at the revisions linked in `source` (secondary: those articles cite the primary reports). No text is copied from them; `note` paraphrases. `firsts` dates the first programs to play a full game (no rating). `breakthroughs` dates five changes in how engines were built, from the same kind of source, for the chart's faint ticks. Made by hand on the date in `retrieved`; experiments/chess/README.md lists the revisions, retrieval times and checksums.
license: The values are facts (ratings, dates, results) taken from Wikipedia articles at the revisions linked; no article text is reproduced. Cite those articles as secondary sources, and the reports they cite as primary.

points.note: Its first rating, after the Massachusetts Amateur Championship; the first program given a chess rating and the first to play in human tournament conditions.
The article puts the average USCF rating of the time near 1500, citing Bill Wall's 'Early Computer Chess Programs'.

points.event: Paul Masson American Class Championships, Class B section, 5-0
points.note: The first time a program won a human tournament section. The Human-computer chess matches article gives the date and puts its rating then at 1722.
Its rating at the time of the tournament, per the article.
The first program to gain a master rating, per the article's timeline.
Ken Thompson and Joe Condon's special-purpose machine at Bell Labs. The same year its USCF rating reached 2250, the first machine rated at master level.
Hans Berliner and Carl Ebeling's machine at Carnegie Mellon; the article calls it the first computer rated over 2400.

points.event: Software Toolworks Championship, shared first with Tony Miles
points.note: The highest performance rating a computer obtained in human play, per the article (USCF scale). Its USCF rating that year was 2551 (Deep Thought article, oldid 1367740918), the highest rating a computer held.

points.event: taken to be the 1997 match with Garry Kasparov, won 3.5-2.5
points.note: The weakest point here: the article gives the figure with no event, no scale and no citation. It describes the machine as searching 200 million positions a second, which is the 1997 machine, so the point is dated to the 1997 match.

firsts.label: first full games
firsts.event: The first programs that play a full game of chess, Alex Bernstein's and one by Russian programmers on a BESM. No rating.

breakthroughs.label: Rybka beta
breakthroughs.event: The first beta of Vasik Rajlich's Rybka is released.

breakthroughs.label: Stockfish Fishtest
breakthroughs.event: Stockfish moves to Fishtest, distributed testing on volunteers' computers; the article credits it with about 120 Elo points in the next twelve months, which took Stockfish to the top of every major rating list.

breakthroughs.label: AlphaZero, Lc0
breakthroughs.event: DeepMind's AlphaZero preprint: a neural network trained by self-play. Leela Chess Zero (Lc0), an open program built on the same method, is first released on 2018-01-09.

breakthroughs.label: Stockfish NNUE
breakthroughs.event: Stockfish 12 is released with NNUE, a neural-network evaluation small enough to run inside its search.

caveats: Human pools, not engine pools. These are ratings earned against people (USCF; Deep Blue's figure states no scale), so they sit on neither the SSDF nor the CCRL scale, and USCF is not FIDE either. The chart draws them apart and never joins them to an engine line.
Two measures. A rating accumulates over many games; a performance rating is one event's result. Most points are performance ratings from five to twelve games, so each is a rough figure.
Secondary sources. Every value is taken from a Wikipedia article at the revision linked, which cites the primary report; none was checked against that report here.
Deep Blue's 2880 has no event, scale or citation in the article it comes from (see its note).
Year-only dates (date_precision 'year') are drawn at July 1 of the year; 'end of 1968' at December 31.
Breakthrough dates are release or announcement dates. A rating list rates a program on its own schedule, often months later, and some never led a list: Houdini never topped an SSDF list.
